item.content:encoded:
For networking and operations teams, a single incident can require evidence from several parts of the private cloud. Gathering that evidence often means moving between management consoles, running diagnostic commands, and checking the results against known issues.

Recent advancements in agentic AI technologies can help evolve network operations by chaining diagnostic reasoning, live telemetry verification, and policy checks into closed-loop investigation workflows. Rather than treating issues as isolated telemetry counters, agents formulate hypotheses, query APIs and CLI endpoints, evaluate evidence across components, and recommend or execute targeted remediations.

This blog explores the use of agentic AI to deliver AI-assisted diagnostics and advisory for networking across VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF). Available as a free-to-download Agentic AI Hub Fling on the Broadcom Support Portal, these specialized agentic workflows assist in investigating networks, flow analysis, and storage issues using live infrastructure tools available through Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations.

What It Does

Agentic AI tools turn an operator’s question into a guided investigation. Domain skills define the checks and tools for each task, while MCP integrations retrieve live inventory, configuration, operational state, and diagnostic results. The assistant brings the findings together and recommends what to check or do next.

The Fling focuses on diagnosis and recommendations, using connectivity probes and diagnostic runbooks to help operators investigate issues. Operators review the findings and decide which configuration changes to make.

Network Diagnostics and Flow Analysis

Network investigations often span NSX Manager, Edge Node diagnostics, and VCF Operations for Networks. Agentic AI brings specialized workflows to some of the most demanding tasks:

  • BGP troubleshooting – Investigate failed or flapping peering sessions using live diagnostic runbooks. Check session state, routes, connectivity, and relevant Edge evidence before recommending a next step.
  • Network Datapath troubleshooting – Investigate connectivity between a source and destination using Traceflow or LiveTrace. Review forwarding observations, identify reported drops, and use the results to guide follow-up checks.
  • Edge and Virtual Network Appliance (VNA) capacity – Examine datapath CPU, memory-pool utilization, and relevant alarms to help assess capacity pressure and sizing needs.
  • NSX upgrade readiness – Review supported upgrade paths, environment health, and pre-checks before a maintenance window. Findings help administrators decide what needs attention before proceeding.
  • Flow analysis – Translate natural-language questions into validated queries for VCF Operations for Networks, then analyze traffic patterns, top talkers, drops, and anomalies.

Consider the question, “Why can’t App-VM-01 reach DB-VM-02 on port 5432?” Agentic AI-based diagnostics can find the endpoint VMs or VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) pods, run the connectivity diagnostic workflow, and report the forwarding observations and any drops it finds. The operator gets evidence about the connection in question, along with follow-up checks and recommendations based on the results.

MCP Servers

The agentic AI agents connect to VCF components through MCP servers. Each server exposes tools that query live inventory, configuration, and operational state, along with prompts that give the model domain context. This grounds the assistant’s reasoning in how each product actually works and in the current state of the environment.

Here’s the list of MCP servers.

Two Ways to Use Agentic AI for Networking

Networking teams can use agentic AI through the built-in UI or connect its MCP tools to an AI client they already work with.

Guided investigations in the UI: Operators sign in through a browser, and the Agent Portal routes each question to the appropriate assistant. The assistants bring domain skills, investigation plans, diagnostic runbooks, and validation rules to the task. Findings can include topology maps, data cards, and charts, with human approval for sensitive tool calls handled in the portal. This is the full built-in assistant experience for operators working through an investigation.

MCP access from other AI harnesses: Teams can connect an MCP-compatible client, such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Gemini CLI, to the Agentic AI MCP endpoint. This approach does not use the built-in assistants. Instead, it gives teams direct access to the MCP tools and resources, which they can build into their own diagnostic workflows and automation. The external client and its model provide the reasoning and workflow; agentic AI platform’s built-in agent skills, investigation plans, guardrail prompts, and rich UI are not included in this approach.

Both options use the same underlying MCP servers, identity framework, role-based tool authorization, and audit logging. Direct MCP access retains those platform access controls, while giving teams flexibility to build their own workflows around the tools.

What Comes Next

The Fling gives customers an opportunity to try these workflows in lab and non-production environments on problems they recognize: a flapping BGP peer, a connection that fails between two applications, or a cluster running short of capacity. Where did the assistant save time? Which checks were missing? Was the recommended next step useful? Those answers will help determine what we improve next.

Areas being explored include vSphere configuration and desired-state inspection, broader lifecycle prechecks, and investigations that connect evidence across compute, networking, and storage. The platform’s modular skills allow our engineering and domain teams to add and refine diagnostic workflows.

Our goal is to provide an agentic AI platform where operators can carry the context of an issue into the specialist diagnostics they need. What we learn through the Fling will help shape that experience and make AI assistance a more useful part of everyday private cloud operations.

Download and learn more on the Broadcom Support Portal.

item.content:encoded:
Introduction

In this part of the series, we will build the two nodes MSSQL FCI Cluster via VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) Automation and its IaaS Services Console.

  • Part 1 focuses on Requirements, Topology and Methods.
  • Part 2 focuses on the Supervisor direct implementation.
  • Part 3 focuses on the VCF Automation manual implementation.
  • Part 4 (this article) focuses on the VCFA Automation blueprint based implementation.

What will you learn from this article?

Compared to parts 2 and 3 where both required manual intervention to be able to provision the nodes. This part turns the project user’s work into one catalog item, where a requester fills in one form, and a VCF Automation takes care of the rest.

By the end of part 4, you will be able to realize the potential of having a blueprint that is ready for provisioning a repeatable infrastructure for MSSQL Server Failover Clustering. This article is not aimed at showcasing how to create the blueprint via the designer, it is more around how the blueprint can be architected to achieve the repeatable state. However you can find the YAML code for this blueprint here.

What does the blueprint focus on?

The blueprint will cover the project user steps mainly. All of the prerequisites from both the Provider Administrator and Organization Administrator must be fulfilled prior to requesting the service.

The Blueprint’s Flow

  • The requester fills in the form and submits it, where all of the required details can be retrieved via VCF Automation directly.
  • VCF Automation evaluates the inputs.
  • Via the Supervisor integration, it creates the Secret and the three volume claims in the namespace, and the vSphere CSI driver creates the shared disks on vSAN.
  • Once all four exist (blueprint conditions), it creates both VMs in parallel.
  • The VM Operator’s webhooks check each VM/
  • NSX binds each typed address to the VM’s port on its subnet.
  • The VM Operator attaches the three disks to both VMs, then powers them on.
  • On the first boot:
    • Sysprep sets the computer name, both addresses with their masks and the password.
    • VCF Automation completes the deployment when both VMs report Created and NetworkReady.

The Request Form

You will see that in the example blueprint design, the form has around 20 fields, and those fields fall into subgroups:

Anatomy of The Blueprint

Similar to what we have showcased in the previous parts, the blueprint will also automate the provisioning up to the level where the nodes are ready for the MSSQL FCI installation.

The blueprint is a simple example and is not the full potential of what can be achieved via VCF Automation, and this is intentional so that you can grab the YAML code and use it in your environment without the need for any complex integration. As such, you will notice that the blueprint’s fields require all static inputs, because dynamic inputs will require VCF Orchestrator workflows, and this is beyond what we set out to do as part of this series.

  • Inputs:
    • Comes first in the file, so the form and the code read in the same order.
    • Every value is typed at request time.
    • There are no hidden variables to edit before you publish.
  • Resources are created in two waves:
    • The first wave holds the Secret and the three volume claims, each ReadWriteMany with the volume mode Block.
    • The second wave holds the two VMs, which depend on all four.
    • Each VM resource waits until VM Operator reports VirtualMachineCreated and VirtualMachineNetworkReady, and only then does VCF Automation mark the deployment complete.
  • Outputs:

Gives the requester a deployment overview with names, addresses and disk sizes, plus the network settings VM Operator actually applied to each interface.

Publishing the Blueprint

After going through the overall logic of the blueprint creation, the next step is to actually create it and then publish it, thus making it available for consumption throughout projects.

  • Go to Build & Deploy -> Content Hub -> Blueprint Design -> and click NEW FROM -> Blank canvas.
  • Name the blueprint and select the project that owns the namespace.
  • Make sure to “Allow all projects in the organization to have access to the catalog item” and “Allow other organizations to have access to the catalog item”.
  • Replace everything in the code editor with the file from the YAML file that was provided previously.
  • The canvas will show the namespace holding the Secret, the three disks and the two VMs, with arrows from each VM to the Secret and the disks.
  • Check that the code editor reports no errors.
  • Click Version, name the version 1.0, select Publish this version to the catalog, and click Create. Once the blueprint is published you will be able to see it available in the Catalog.

Consuming the Blueprint

Now that the blueprint is published, it can be requested in order to provision the two nodes that will be hosting the MSSQL FCI deployment.

  • Go to Build & Deploy -> Catalog -> and click on REQUEST within the published catalog item.
  • Fill in the form with the values (you can easily get the values from our deployment in Part 3).
  • Submit the request and follow the deployment.
  • When it completes, the overview lists the names and addresses, and the outputs.
  • Once each VM’s GuestCustomization is complete you sign in to Windows, and start working on the MSSQL prerequisites and deployments from an application level perspective.

Summary

Now that we’re at the end of this series, we have showcased how the VM Service can be  consumed to provision the infrastructure for business critical applications such as Microsoft SQL Server Failover Cluster Instance(s), and we went through the different methods for achieving this. Thank you for taking the time to learn and engage with us.

item.content:encoded:
At a Glance:

  • 500 Clusters per Control Plane: Single Supervisor scale increases from 190 to 500 clusters, eliminating fragmented management planes.
  • 70% Faster Provisioning: Fast Deploy leverages per-datastore caching and linked-mode delta disks to cut cluster provisioning from 37 to 11 minutes and upgrade times by 75%.
  • Multi-NIC and Cilium Support: Isolate data and control planes, enable native multicast for streaming/finance feeds, and run Cilium via a managed CNI Addon Framework.
  • Unified VM and Container Primitives: Manage boot-sequenced VM groups, Day-2 network mutability, and lightweight vSphere Pods directly on ESXi without full cluster overhead.
  • Turnkey GitOps: Native supervisor integration with Argo CD and Harbor lets you declare both infrastructure and apps via Git.
  • Free Lab Access: Test the core capabilities with the HOL-2704-07 lab.

If you are a Platform Engineer or SRE, you already know the pain of “Day 2” Kubernetes operations. What often starts as an initiative to speed up innovation quickly degrades into managing infrastructure silos, wrestling with fragmented toolchains, and bridging widening skill gaps. Scaling enterprise-grade clusters reliably while keeping developers happy is no small feat.

Enter VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS). With recent releases, the focus has shifted heavily toward developer autonomy, massive scalability, and eliminating operational toil.

To help practitioners get under the hood of these new capabilities, VMware has released a comprehensive Hands-on Lab HOL-2704-07 | Hands-on with Kubernetes: Deep Dive With the vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.6. Below is a breakdown of the architectural shifts that matter most to SREs, a look at the latest VKS 3.8 release, and how you can test the platform firsthand.

Architectural Highlights for Platform Engineers

1. Unprecedented Scale and “Fast Deploy” Speed

Managing cluster sprawl just got significantly easier. You can now scale up to 500 VKS clusters per supervisor control plane—a massive leap from the 190 limit in previous versions. Furthermore, VKS ships with upstream-aligned Kubernetes and 24 months of enterprise support, providing stability and reducing mandatory upgrade churn.

For SREs managing dynamic capacity or sudden traffic spikes, Fast Deploy is the real star. By combining per-datastore image caching and delta-disk technology (Linked Mode), cluster provisioning time drops by 70% (from 37 minutes down to 11 minutes), and cluster upgrade time is cut by 75%.

2. Extensible Networking and CNI Freedom

Historically, routing all cluster management, API traffic, and data planes through a single interface created critical performance bottlenecks. VKS introduces a multi-network architecture supporting multiple vNICs per worker node and pod:

  • Native Multicast Support: Run real-time streaming and financial feeds directly inside VKS.
  • Control/Data Plane Isolation: Decouple high-throughput application data planes from the Kubernetes control plane to eliminate noisy-neighbor issues.
  • Direct Hardware Access: Use SR-IOV for low-latency, line-rate throughput without hypervisor software encapsulation.

On top of this, the CNI Addon Framework ends CNI lock-in. While Antrea and Calico remain supported out of the box, you can now deploy a managed Cilium add-on package during cluster provisioning without breaking VKS lifecycle boundaries.

3. Workload Flexibility: VMs and Containers Under One API

The platform unifies VMs, Kubernetes clusters, and raw containers under a single declarative framework:

  • Day-2 Network Mutability: Modify, add, or delete VM network interfaces after deployment through the UI or API without rebuilding the workload (requiring only a simple reboot).
  • VM Service Groups: Group sets of VMs together for orchestrated bulk actions, including staged power-on “waves” with configurable boot delays (e.g., ensuring a database tier initializes before web frontends).
  • vSphere Pod Container Service: For lightweight or legacy workloads that don’t justify a full Kubernetes cluster overhead, run isolated containers directly on ESXi nodes using vSphere Pods. They execute in a lightweight VM boundary (CRX) for hardware-level isolation, bypassing the guest OS layer entirely.

4. Native GitOps with Argo CD and Harbor

Declarative infrastructure is standard practice for modern platform engineering. Argo CD, Harbor, and GitLab integrate as Supervisor services. You can manage both cluster lifecycle manifests and application overlays directly from a Git repository, letting Argo CD reconcile desired infrastructure and workload states automatically.

What You Learn in the Hands-on Lab (HOL-2704-07-VCF-L)

The lab provides a preconfigured sandbox that walks through the core platform features over five distinct modules:

Flexible, Self-Paced Access: You can start this lab at any point and complete the modules in any order; the modules are not dependent on one another. You can also exit and come back to the lab as often as you like.

By significantly reducing the Day-2 operational burden, VKS allows platform teams to step away from routine maintenance and focus on accelerating business outcomes.

Beyond the Lab: What’s New in VKS 3.8

While the Hands-on Lab gives you a robust sandbox for VKS 3.6, VMware has already released VKS 3.8 to further accelerate AI workloads and tighten security baselines. As detailed in the recent VKS 3.8 announcement, this latest release introduces several major capabilities:

  • Automated Chained Upgrades: VKS 3.8 eliminates multi-hop upgrade scripting by orchestrating multi-version vSphere Kubernetes release upgrades automatically with built-in dependency checks. The system cordons and drains pods from worker nodes just once during the entire process, drastically reducing maintenance windows.
  • Platform Hardening and Security Guardrails: SSH access is programmatically disabled across all Kubernetes control plane and worker nodes to elevate the security baseline. Additionally, an Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment (AIDE) periodically performs integrity checks across critical system directories to detect tampering.
  • Granular Workload Placement: Platform teams can programmatically pin workloads to specific resources based on infrastructure policy. This allows you to explicitly exclude high-cost hardware (like dedicated GPUs) from control plane node scheduling or assign distinct node pools to specific sites for active-active stretched clusters.
  • Centralized Credential Governance: The External Secrets Operator (ESO) add-on now dynamically synchronizes credentials from enterprise vaults like HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, and GCP Secret Manager. This simplifies compliance audits and eliminates plain-text secrets in Git repositories and YAML manifests.
  • Native CI/CD Pipelines: VKS 3.8 introduces Tekton for in-cluster continuous integration (CI) pipelines to automate code builds and testing without exposing clusters to external networks. These pipelines sync natively with Argo CD for continuous global fleet delivery.
  • Kubernetes 1.37 Support: Decoupling its release cadence from core platform upgrades, VKS 3.8 supports Kubernetes 1.37 within 60 days of upstream releases, backed by Broadcom’s 24 months of extended support.

Ready to get hands-on?

  • Test the core capabilities: Launch the free HOL-2704-07 | Hands-on with Kubernetes: Deep Dive With the vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.6 lab.
  • First time user? Follow this Create an HOL Account Guide to get registered.
  • Explore more: Browse the full catalog of 90+ labs at labs.hol.vmware.com.

item.content:encoded:
Introduction

In this part of the series, we will build the two nodes MSSQL FCI Cluster via VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) Automation and its IaaS Services Console.

  • Part 1 focuses on Requirements, Topology and Methods.
  • Part 2 focuses on the Supervisor direct implementation.
  • Part 3 (this article) focuses on the VCF Automation manual implementation.
  • Part 4 focuses on the VCFA Automation blueprint based implementation

What will you learn from this article?

By the end of part 3, you will be able to create a fully fledged infrastructure that is ready for MSSQL Server Failover Clustering via VCF Automation Manually.

The Configuration Iteration

Moving to VCF Automation is not just a simple abstraction of the Supervisor. It is a shift from the individual vSphere Administrator persona to the multi-tenancy personas. However, the data plane remains the same and the service layers will also remain the same.

VCF Automation does not change the MSSQL cluster; it changes the operating model, where:

  • The provider decides what an organization may use.
  • The organization administrator packages it within the context of Namespace(s).
  • The project user builds inside the Namespace packaging/limits/resources.

Step 01: Provider Administrator

The first person is the Provider Administrator, given that the region(s) were created, there is an additional configuration item that needs to be taken care of before proceeding to the organization configuration, and this is the Infrastructure Policy:

  • A Compute Policy must be pre-created in the vCenter, this could be a VM-to-VM anti-affinity, or VM-to-Host anti-affinity, depending on your requirements to separate. Either for extra availability, or for extra availability and licensing placement perhaps.
  • Via the Provider Portal -> Infrastructure Policies -> Create a new Infrastructure Policy.
  • Now given that the Organization has been created and provided with its region resources and networking capabilities:
    • Go to Organizations, select the organization, and open its Region Quota:
      • Make sure that you have configured the reservations in the assigned region quota, otherwise the Organization administrator will not be able to see the sql-fci-8c64g VM Class.
      • Theb optionally -> Under Infrastructure Policies, click Edit and add the newly created policy.

Step 02: Organization Administrator

Continuing with the second persona, the Organization Administrator will now prepare the organization level resources that will be consumed by the Project User(s).

  • Start by creating a Content Library if you haven’t done so, and then upload the Windows image to it.
    • Login as an Organization Administrator -> Build & Deploy -> Content Hub -> Content Libraries -> New.
    • Once the Content Library is created, click on it -> VM Images -> Upload.
  • Now on to the Namespace creation:
    • Go to Manage & Govern -> Namespace Class -> click New.
    • Set CPU and Memory limits and reservations that cover both nodes with room to spare (remember the VM class requirements).
    • Add the VM class sql-fci-8c64g.Add the storage class (policy).
    • Click Create.
  • Next will be the creation of the project:
    • Go to Manage & Govern -> Projects -> click on NEW and create a new project.
    • Once the project is created -> click on the project -> go to the Namespaces tab -> click on NEW NAMESPACE:
      • Provide the name for the Namespace.
      • Choose the namespace class.
      • Choose the region and check the zone added.
      • Choose the VPC type:
        • If the subnets were pre-created/existing, you add them directly in this phase.
        • If the subnets need to be created, you can create them later on after the Namespace creation is done.
        • Click Create (do note that VCF Automation adds a short suffix to the name, for example mssqlfci-prod-x7k2q, so use the full name from here on).
        • For the Infrastructure Policy, this can be added after the Namespace has been created by clicking on the Namespace name and scrolling down to Infrastructure Policies -> ADD, afterwards this will show when the VMs are going to be created.

Step 03: Project User (IaaS Services Console):

For the final persona, it is the role of the Project User(s) to start creating the required resources to build the MSSQL nodes.

  • A – Create the network subnets

If the subnets were not previously created and added to the Namespace as previously explained, then you will need to create the two primary and heartbeat subnets from within the Namespace itself.

  • Go to Build & Deploy -> Namespace that you have created -> Network -> Subnets -> NEW SUBNET, you will notice that the same UI and fields that were present to you via the Supervisor, are also present here via VCF Automation, so that there is consistency in terms of consuming those services.
  • B – Create the shared Volumes

For this specific deployment, the shared disks number, volume and sizes are there to serve the purpose of showcasing how it works, however in production, most likely you will have a completely different number of disks with different sizes and allocations based on your requirements.

  • Go to Build & Deploy -> Namespace that you have created -> Volume -> NEW VOLUME, you will notice that the same UI and fields that were present to you via the Supervisor, are also present here via VCF Automation, so that there is consistency in terms of consuming those services.
  • C – Create the VMs

We will be creating the two nodes, without attaching the Shared Volumes during creation, this step will be done later on (the following steps are to be repeated per VM):

  • Go to Build & Deploy -> Namespace that you have created -> Virtual Machine -> CREATE VM, you will notice that the same UI and fields that were present to you via the Supervisor, are also present here via VCF Automation, so that there is consistency in terms of consuming those services.
  • Pick the source type from where you will deploy this VM: choose OVF
  • Select the VM Class and VM Image:
    • Input the VM’s name.
    • Select the zone.
    • Select the Windows 2022 image.
    • Select the VM class.
    • Select the Storage Class
    • Change the Power State to Powered Off.
  • Advanced Settings (optional): you can configure Sysprep here if desired, otherwise skip to the next configuration window.
  • Network Configuration:
    • Edit the default eth0 interface and select the primary network and input the IP address.
    • Click on ADD NETWORK INTERFACE and select the heartbeat network and input the IP address.
    • Fill in the Global Network Settings as desired.
    • Review and confirm.
  • D – Attach the Shared Volumes

We will be attaching the three volumes that were created previously, and this action will be repeated on the two VMs.

  • Go to Build & Deploy -> Namespace that you have created -> Virtual Machine -> click on the MSSQL node VM, you will notice that the same UI and fields that were present to you via the Supervisor, are also present here via VCF Automation, so that there is consistency in terms of consuming those services.
  • Scroll down to Volumes.
  • Click on “ATTACH VOLUME”.
  • Select Choose from existing volumes, select sqlfci01-data and set Application Type to Microsoft WSFC.
  • Repeat the same steps for sqlfci01-home, then for sqlfci01-quorum (keep the order on both nodes).
  • E – Power On the VMs

Now that everything is set, you can change the state of the VMs from Powered Off to Powered On.

  • Go to Build & Deploy -> Namespace that you have created -> Virtual Machine -> click on the MSSQL node VM, you will notice that the same UI and fields that were present to you via the Supervisor, are also present here via VCF Automation, so that there is consistency in terms of consuming those services.
  • Toggle the Power State so that to change it to Powered On.
  • Repeat the same steps for the second MSSQL node VM.

MSSQL FCI Installation

From here you can work on the initial configuration of the Windows OS, and then follow Microsoft’s guidance for installing and configuring a two node Microsoft SQL Server Failover Cluster.

Up Next

Head over to Part 4, where we will build on the same topology via VCF Automation via the Blueprint Designer so that this can be consumed as a repeatable service for all project users without having to go through the manual iteration.

Series · Part 3 of 6
The VCF 9.1 VPC Networking Mental Model
1VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 1: From External Connection to VPC
2VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 2: IP Blocks, External Connections, Transit Gateways, Subnets, and NAT
3VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 3: The Distributed Transit GatewayYou are here
4VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 4: VLAN Extension Under the HoodComing soon
5VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 5: Four Gates for VPC TrafficComing soon
6VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 6: The VPC North-South Firewall and Its CoverageComing soon

This is Part 3 of the series The VCF 9.1 VPC Networking Mental Model. Part 2 built the routing model: IP blocks, External Connections, Transit Gateways, Connectivity Profiles, and subnet access modes. It closed with a short warning that VLAN extension serves a different purpose. This part opens the hood on the gateway that makes it possible: the Distributed Transit Gateway (DTGW).

Two questions drive everything discussed below. How does a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) reach the physical network with no NSX Edge and no routing protocol? And how can a VPC subnet share one broadcast domain with a VLAN that already has servers and a gateway on it? This part answers the first. Part 4, coming soon, will answer the second.

Core idea

A DTGW is one logical gateway that NSX builds on every ESX host. It is attached to an external VLAN whose CIDR already contains the VPC’s External IP block. So the physical router sees VPC addresses as directly connected. VLAN extension reuses the same Distributed VLAN Connection object but dedicates it to a single subnet, so that subnet and an existing VLAN become one Layer 2 domain with one CIDR and one physical gateway.

In everyday terms, picture a supermarket. A centralized gateway is one big checkout by the main door. Every shopper queues there. A distributed transit gateway puts a till at the end of every aisle, so shoppers pay and leave from wherever they are. Only special requests, like returns, still go to the service desk. That desk is the VNA. VLAN extension is different. It knocks a doorway through to the old shop next door, so both share one floor while the stock moves across.

1. What a DTGW really is

A Transit Gateway becomes distributed the moment you attach it to a distributed external connection. The result is a gateway instantiated on each ESX host, with no NSX Edge nodes in the path. Traffic that needs no stateful services runs at close to physical NIC line rate.

Three properties fall out of that design. Each one has a design consequence.

  • Every host is an exit. North-south traffic leaves on the host where the VM runs. There is no Edge to hair-pin through and no Edge to size. The price is that the external VLAN must be present on every host in the span, on the same VDS uplinks as the host TEPs.
  • East-west is still overlay. VM-to-VM traffic between hosts rides GENEVE between TEPs, as before. The external VLAN is only for traffic entering or leaving the VPC domain.
  • Stateful services need a home. Stateful services such as NAT cannot be distributed to the hosts. They run on a Virtual Network Appliance (VNA) cluster. The VPC Gateway’s north-south services are instantiated there, and the VNA must sit inside the external VLAN span.

All external connections on one Transit Gateway must be the same type, all centralized or all distributed. A project can have several DTGWs. They may share a VLAN or use different ones, but public subnets and External IPs must not overlap between DTGWs.

2. The on-link trick: why no BGP and no static routes

A centralized connection needs a Tier-0 gateway on NSX Edge nodes with external routing, such as BGP, to the fabric. A DTGW has none of that. So how does the physical router know where 10.50.0.70 lives?

The answer is one design rule: the External IP block must sit inside the external VLAN’s CIDR. The Transit Gateway wizard says so on the form: “The External IP Block must be within the Gateway CIDR”. In the lab the external VLAN is 150 with 10.50.0.0/24, and the External IP block is 10.50.0.64/26, a slice of that /24.

One thing to know: NSX does not stop you if you break this rule. In the lab, a block of 30.30.30.0/24, which sits in no external VLAN, was added to the connectivity profile and a Public subnet was carved from it. Both saved with status Success. The physical switch has no route to those addresses, so return traffic for that subnet never arrives. Keeping the block inside the VLAN CIDR is your job, not the UI’s.

Think of the external VLAN as one /24 with two owners. The core switch owns the gateway, 10.50.0.1, and sees the whole /24 as a connected route. NSX owns the slice you gave it, 10.50.0.64/26, and answers for every address it hands out from that slice. When the switch needs to reach 10.50.0.70, it does what it does for any host on a connected subnet: it ARPs on VLAN 150, and the DTGW replies. No static route and no BGP are needed, because the address was never outside the switch’s own subnet.

What the external VLAN’s addresses are used for

A common question: is the external VLAN only for Public subnets? No. Public subnets are one of four things NSX carves out of the External IP block. The VLAN itself is a transit network. VMs only get an address from it when they sit on a Public subnet, and even then the subnet is an overlay segment, not the VLAN.

What uses VLAN 150’s addresses How much it takes Example
The physical gateway and anything physical on the VLAN Kept out of the External IP block 10.50.0.1, plus devices in .2 to .63
Public subnet A whole small subnet carved from the block 10.50.0.64/28 for ip-man-a-web, 10.50.0.80/28 for ip-man-b-web
External IP (1:1 NAT for one private VM) One address from the block 10.50.0.100
Default outbound NAT (needs a VNA) One address per VPC from the block 10.50.0.120
Load balancer VIP One address per VIP from the block Any free address in the block
Private-VPC and Private-TGW subnets Nothing. They never appear on VLAN 150 172.16.0.0/26, 172.20.0.0/26

Everything NSX puts on the external VLAN comes from the External IP block. The two Public subnets are from the lab. The single addresses are the examples used in Figure 8 below.

Do not confuse this with VLAN extension in Part 4. A transit VLAN like 150 is carved into small pieces and shared by many VPCs. An extended VLAN is a workload VLAN, and its whole CIDR becomes one subnet.

Adding another external VLAN

If VLAN 150 still has free addresses, you do not need a new VLAN. Add another CIDR from inside 10.50.0.0/24 to the External IP block. You only need a second VLAN when the first one is full or you want a separate exit. The rule stays the same: each VLAN gets its own Distributed VLAN connection, and each External IP block sits inside the VLAN it belongs to. This was tested in the lab with VLAN 160 (10.51.0.0/24):

  1. In the Default project, create a Distributed VLAN connection for VLAN 160 with gateway 10.51.0.1/24. Leave Dedicated to Subnet off.
  2. Create an External IP block inside that VLAN, 10.51.0.64/26.
  3. Share the new connection and the new block with the project.
  4. Edit the DTGW and add the new connection next to the existing one. The DTGW now has two Distributed VLAN connections.
  5. Add the new block to the VPC Connectivity Profile.
  6. When you create a Public subnet, the IP Block field now lists both blocks. Pick the one for the VLAN you want.

The physical side needs the same as VLAN 150: VLAN 160 trunked to every host in the span and an SVI at 10.51.0.1. The lab did not show how NSX chooses between two exits for traffic leaving the VPC, so check the Broadcom docs for that.

The Broadcom tech docs state the requirement. Set up Distributed Network Connectivity says External IP blocks must be the same as, or a subset of, the dedicated VLAN subnets. The VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1 design guide adds that public subnet addresses, External IPs, translated NAT addresses and load balancer VIPs are presented to the external VLAN through the host uplinks where the TEPs are.

Three rules from the docs matter most in production:

  • Exclude anything already in use. The gateway IP is excluded automatically. Every other address used by a physical device or VM on that VLAN must be excluded from the External IP block with an exclude range. Otherwise NSX can hand it to a VPC and you get a duplicate IP.
  • Expect asymmetry from on-link neighbours. Traffic between a device sitting directly on the external VLAN and VPC addresses from the External IP block can be asymmetric. Keep the external VLAN for transit, not for servers.
  • Set up the external gateway as documented. Turn off ICMP redirects on the external VLAN gateway. Make sure it forwards a packet that arrived from one ESX host on that VLAN back out to the same host or a different one.

The payoff is operational. Once the VLAN and its gateway exist, new VPCs, public subnets, External IPs and VIPs need zero change in the physical network. To grow, you have two levers. A connectivity profile takes up to five External IP blocks, and the project’s Set External IP Blocks dialog shows “Maximum 5 IP Blocks”. One IP block can also hold several CIDRs. The lab saved a block with eleven, and the NSX API reference lists no maximum for that field. For the supported numbers, check the Broadcom configuration maximums. Whichever lever you use, each CIDR must still sit inside an external VLAN CIDR.

3. Three north-south paths

Not every packet takes the same road out. The access mode of the source subnet decides it.

Source What happens Appliance in the path?
Public subnet Routed by the local VPC Gateway and DTGW. Leaves the host on the external VLAN with its real IP. No
Private subnet VM with an External IP Stateless 1:1 NAT in the host data path, then out the same way. No
Private-VPC or Private-TGW, no External IP Default Outbound NAT (Auto-SNAT), custom NAT or 1:N SNAT on the VNA cluster. Yes, the VNA

Only traffic sourced from private or Private-TGW subnets is sent to the VNA cluster for stateful services such as NAT. So a VNA is optional. If you only need public subnets, External IPs and Avi load balancing, you do not need one. Auto-SNAT, custom NAT, the VNA load balancer and (from 9.1.1) DHCP relay to an external server all require it, with N-S Services enabled in the connectivity profile.

What the VM uses as its gateway

A Public subnet’s addresses come from VLAN 150’s range, so it is tempting to give the VMs 10.50.0.1 as their gateway. Do not. Every VPC subnet has its own gateway on the VPC Gateway, and NSX sets it to the first usable address of the subnet. The VM only ever talks to that address. 10.50.0.1 is the DTGW’s next hop, not the VM’s.

Follow a VM at 10.50.0.70 on that Public subnet out to the data centre:

Hop Who Next hop
1 The VM, 10.50.0.70/28 Its default gateway, 10.50.0.65 on the VPC Gateway. The VPC Gateway runs on every host, so this hop never leaves the host.
2 VPC Gateway The DTGW, over an internal link from the VPC Transit Subnets range on the DTGW (100.64.0.0/21 by default). VMs never see these addresses.
3 DTGW 10.50.0.1, the gateway entered in the Distributed VLAN connection, out the host uplink on VLAN 150.
Return Core switch 10.50.0.70 is on its connected /24, so it ARPs on VLAN 150 and the DTGW answers.

The VM sees a /28 with gateway .65. The switch sees the same address as a host on its /24. Both views are right, because the DTGW sits between them.

Private subnets work the same way at hop 1. A VM on 172.16.0.0/26 uses 172.16.0.1, and a Private-TGW VM uses the first address of its own subnet. The difference comes later, as the table above shows: an External IP is translated on the host, and anything else goes to the VNA for SNAT before it reaches VLAN 150.

Worked example: one external VLAN, many subnets

Here is the whole thing end to end. One DTGW, one external VLAN 150 (10.50.0.0/24, gateway 10.50.0.1 on the core switch) and an External IP block of 10.50.0.64/26. VPC-A has a public subnet with a web VM at 10.50.0.70, a private subnet with an app VM at 172.16.10.10 that owns External IP 10.50.0.100, and a second private subnet with a db VM at 172.16.20.10 and no External IP. VPC-B has a public subnet with a VM at 10.50.0.85. On the physical side there is exactly one thing configured for all of this: the SVI on VLAN 150.

The distributed external connection sets 10.50.0.1 as the default gateway for the external VLAN. The core switch sees VLAN 150 as a connected /24. Now follow the four flows.

  • The web VM on the public subnet: 10.50.0.70 comes from the External IP block, which sits inside VLAN 150’s CIDR. For the core switch it is an address in a directly connected subnet. NSX presents public subnet addresses to the external VLAN through the host uplinks where the TEPs are. Nothing is translated and no appliance is in the path.
  • The app VM on a private subnet with an External IP: its traffic uses a stateless 1:1 NAT between 172.16.10.10 and 10.50.0.100. External IPs are presented to the external VLAN the same way as public subnet addresses, so inbound connections to 10.50.0.100 work too. No appliance is in the path.
  • The db VM on a private subnet with no External IP: to reach the outside it needs Default Outbound NAT (Auto-SNAT), which is a stateful service. Traffic from a private subnet is forwarded to the VNA cluster, which translates it to an address from the External IP block (10.50.0.120 in the figure). This is the only flow in the example that uses an appliance. It needs a VNA cluster and N-S Services.
  • The VPC-B VM to the web VM, east-west between VPCs: east-west traffic between workloads is carried by GENEVE between the host TEPs. It does not use VLAN 150 or the core switch.

Two things follow. First, the only addresses that appear on VLAN 150 are the gateway and addresses from the External IP block: public subnet addresses, External IPs, translated NAT addresses and load balancer VIPs. 172.16.x.x never leaves the VPC. Second, adding VPC-C, ten more private subnets or another public subnet changes nothing on the core switch, as long as every public address comes from the block. The only reason to touch the physical network again is a new exit, which section 7 of Part 4, coming soon, covers.

What’s next

Part 4, coming soon, picks up the second question: how a VPC subnet and an existing VLAN become one broadcast domain. It covers the four objects behind VLAN extension, Layer 2 versus Layer 2 plus Layer 3, how many external connections you really need, the migration workflow and the TEP-less VLAN-backed VPC.

item.content:encoded:
Introduction

In this part of the series, we will build the two nodes MSSQL FCI Cluster via the vSphere Supervisor and the Local Consumption Interface service.

  • Part 1 focuses on Requirements, Topology, and Methods.
  • Part 2 (this article) focuses on the Supervisor Direct Implementation.
  • Part 3 focuses on the VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) Automation manual implementation.
  • Part 4 focuses on the VCF Automation blueprint-based implementation.

What will you learn from this article?

By the end of part 2, you will be able to create a fully fledged infrastructure that is ready for MSSQL Server Failover Clustering via the Supervisor VM Service.

The Configuration Iteration

To achieve the desired configuration, we will iterate between the vCenter vSphere Client and the Supervisor’s Local Consumption Interface.

For the sake of keeping this realistic, we will put some assumptions for the configuration values, which will be used to represent the different iteration inputs.

Step 01: Check the shared-disk capability

Shared disks work only when the Supervisor capability “supports_shared_disks_with_VM_service_VMs” is active, and this is set to true by default, however it is always good to double check.

By using VCF CLI, make sure you are on the Supervisor default context then you can use kubectl to retrieve the capability state, where the expected output is “true”:

<strong>kubectl get capabilities.iaas.vmware.com supervisor-capabilities -o jsonpath='{.status.supervisor.supports_shared_disks_with_VM_service_VMs.activated}'</strong>

On the other hand, when this is set to “false,” the VM Operator removes the shared-disk fields from its API, and the later steps fail.

Step 02: Create the storage policy

Depending on your performance preference, and the actual production MSSQL deployment requirements, you should configure a storage policy to match those requirements. One thing to note: “VM Encryption” cannot be added to-date, and if configured the VM Operator will refuse adding a shared controller on an encrypted storage class. To that end, you may use an alternative, such as. vSAN’s data-at-rest encryption.

Step 03: Create the VM Class

The VM Class here is important, not just from a t-shirt size perspective, but also from a performance perspective, given that creating the VM Class includes configuring the compute criteria required by the MSSQL nodes.

  • From the Supervisor Management, go to the Services tab, and click Manage on the VM Service pane. Click VM Classes, then Create VM Class.
  • Name it, i.e. sql-fci-8c64g, and make sure you’re picking the newest virtual hardware version as this cannot be changed later.
  • Finish the wizard, then open the class and click Edit:
    • Set CPU to 8 and memory to 64 GB.
    • Set the memory reservation to 64 GB and tick Reserve all guest memory (All locked).
    • Leave CPU Hot Plug and Memory Hot Plug unchecked.
  • Under VM Options, Boot Options, choose EFI firmware and enable Secure Boot.
  • An important note: Make sure you’re not adding any new SCSI controllers; those will be added automatically by the VM Operator when the shared disks are attached.

Step 04: Prepare the vSphere Namespace

After configuring the storage policy and the VM Class, and given that you already have a content library that has the Windows 2022 template, it is time to create the Namespace.

  • From the Supervisor Management, go to Namespaces and create the namespace sql-prod in the Supervisor’s designated zone.
  • On the namespace:
    • From the Storage card, add the RAID-5 policy (which will appear in the namespace as a storage class).
    • From the VM Service card:
      • Click Add VM Class and select sql-fci-8c64g.
      • Click Add Content Library and select the library that holds the Windows image.

Step 05: Create the Subnets

The configuration requires the creation of the primary and heartbeat networks, and to that end there are multiple ways:

  • If it is a shared subnet, as in not originating from the Namespace and was created via NSX to serve other workloads, then what you need to do is attach the subnets to the Namespace rather than creating them:
    • From the Supervisor Management, go to sql-prod Namespace and select the Configure tab (give it a couple of seconds to load all the information).
    • In General, scroll down to the Namespace Networks, and click on Add.
    • Once you have added both networks, they will show as “Shared Namespace Network” in the UI.
  • If the subnet will be originating from the Namespace directly, those can be configured via the Local Consumption Interface:
    • From the Supervisor Management, go to sql-prod Namespace and select the Resources tab.
    • Click on “GO TO SERVICE” in the Network card.
    • Click on the Subnets tab.
    • Click on “NEW SUBNET”, and from here the first time you will create the public network, and you will do the same to create the private heartbeat network.
    • Those networks will be bound to the Namespace and will not be marked as shared.

Step 06: Create the shared volumes

For this specific deployment, the shared disks number, volume and sizes are there to serve the purpose of showcasing how it works, however in production, most likely you will have a completely different number of disks with different sizes and allocations based on your requirements.

  • From the Supervisor Management, go to sql-prod Namespace and select the Resources tab.
  • Click on “GO TO SERVICE” in the Volume card, and click New Volume, then you are going to create the following three volumes:

Step 07: Create the VMs

We will be creating the two nodes, without attaching the Shared Volumes during creation, this step will be done later on (the following steps are to be repeated per VM):

  • From the Supervisor Management, go to sql-prod Namespace and select the Resources tab.
  • Click on “GO TO SERVICE” in the Virtual Machine Service card, and click CREATE VM.
  • Pick the source type from where you will deploy this VM: choose OVF
  • Select the VM Class and VM Image:
    • Input the VM’s name.
    • Select the zone.
    • Select the Windows 2022 image.
    • Select the VM class.
    • Select the Storage Class
    • Change the Power State to Powered Off.
  • Advanced Settings (optional): you can configure Sysprep here if desired, otherwise skip to the next configuration window.
  • Network Configuration:
    • Edit the default eth0 interface and select the primary network and input the IP address.
    • Click on ADD NETWORK INTERFACE and select the heartbeat network and input the IP address.
    • Fill in the Global Network Settings as desired.
  • Review and confirm.

Step 08: Attach the Shared Volumes

We will be attaching the 3 volumes that were created previously, and this action will be repeated on the two VMs.

  • From the Supervisor Management, go to sql-prod Namespace and select the Resources tab.
  • Click on “GO TO SERVICE” in the Virtual Machine Service card.
  • Click on the MSSQL node VM.
  • Scroll down to Volumes.
  • Click on “ATTACH VOLUME”.
  • Select Choose from existing volumes, select sqlfci01-data and set Application Type to Microsoft WSFC.
  • Repeat the same steps for sqlfci01-home, then for sqlfci01-quorum (keep the order on both nodes).
  • For you to see also the controller, you can edit the VM settings in the vSphere Client (you’ll get a warning so that you do not to modify anything). From there you can see the additional SCSI controller that has been added and you can see that all 3 volumes/disks are now attached to it.

Step 09: Power On the VMs

Now that everything is set, you can change the state of the VMs from Powered Off to Powered On.

  • From the Supervisor Management, go to sql-prod Namespace and select the Resources tab.
  • Click on “GO TO SERVICE” in the Virtual Machine Service card.
  • Click on the first MSSQL node VM.
  • Toggle the Power State so that to change it to Powered On.
  • Repeat the same steps for the second MSSQL node VM.

Step 10: Create the DRS Rules

Finally you can configure a DRS rule which makes sure that both nodes do not reside on the same ESX host at the same time.

Step 11: MSSQL FCI Installation

From here you can work on the initial configuration of the Windows OS, and then follow Microsoft’s guidance for installing and configuring a two node Microsoft SQL Server Failover Cluster.

Up Next

Head over to Part 3, where we will build on the same topology via VCF Automation via the IaaS Services Console.

Introduction

The transition to VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) will typically involve questions about not only new functionalities, but also functionalities and capabilities that are already in use. One of the most common use cases for vSphere is virtualizing business-critical applications (BCA). Running these applications on vSphere is a well-established, industry-validated practice with widespread adoption. With VCF, the Supervisor and its VM Service capability, the question was whether we can run BCA on top of a Supervisor VM Service. The answer is YES!

This multi-part series will focus on the design and implementation of Microsoft SQL Failover Cluster Instances (FCI) on top of VCF 9.x. From the basic Supervisor deployment to a fully fledged VCF Automation blueprint, we will go through the different requirements alongside their architectural impact and then finally walk you through the implementation steps.

  • Part 1 (this article) focuses on Requirements, Topology and Methods.
  • Part 2 focuses on the Supervisor direct implementation.
  • Part 3 focuses on the VCF Automation manual implementation.
  • Part 4 focuses on the VCFA Automation blueprint based implementation.

What will you learn from this article?

By the end of part 1, you will be able to identify what is required to build the infrastructure side of the MSSQL FCIs, including mapping the traditional VM objects to VM Service objects. In addition, you will be able to describe the topologies that will be used to build the platform, which will be covered in parts 2-4.

Traditional VMs Versus VM Service

Before going further, we will map out and compare a standard MSSQL VM versus a VM Service based MSSQL VM.

MSSQL FCI Cluster Requirements

A Windows Server Failover Cluster (WSFC) is a group of Windows Servers that provides logically a since service that is highly-available, where if one node fails, another takes over. For MSSQL FCI, the active node will own the shared disks, the MSSQL cluster computer object which relatively owns the MSSQL cluster listener. The following table details what will be required from the platform to achieve this:

The Building Blocks (based on VCF 9.1.1)

High-Level Architecture

This high-level architecture includes the aspects related only to MSSQL FCI use case, and it will not cover aspects that are related to VCF Fleet, Instances or Workload Domains. In addition, the high-level architecture focuses primarily on the data plane, where the other parts of the series will cover achieving the same use case across the different management planes.

General Overview

Like any vSphere Namespace, this one has its quote allocated, storage policies defined, VM Classes and Content Library assigned. From a networking standpoint, each node has two network interfaces:

  • NIC 1 is connected to sql-public which is the client-facing subnet, and its default gateway leads through the VPC’s transit gateway to the clients. The term public (which is also referred to as primary) here means client-facing, and from an NSX terminology the subnet can use the Private – Transit Gateway access mode, or Public when the addresses must be routable outside the organization.
  • NIC 2 is connected to sql-heartbeat, which is the private subnet that stays inside the VPC and has no gateway.

On the storage side, both nodes reach the same three disks through SCSI controller 1 (SCSI controller 0 will be used by the OS disk(s) by default), which uses physical bus sharing (the sizes/values are just examples):

  • sqlfci01-data (500 GB) is attached at SCSI 1:0 and holds the user databases.
  • sqlfci01-home (100 GB) is attached at SCSI 1:1 and holds the SQL Server instance files and system databases.
  • sqlfci01-quorum (50 GB) attached at SCSI 1:2 and acts as the cluster’s disk witness.

A caveat with respect to having shared volumes/disks, that they must be kept within the zone and mapped to one vSAN cluster. Although in VCF 9.1 a zone can span several clusters, a vSAN datastore belongs to one cluster, and both nodes must access the same datastore where the volumes/disks will be residing.

Shared Volumes

Since this is a core area across the entire series, we needed to go through more details around it.

  • It all starts with the volume creation, and in the Supervisor world, this is translated into a persistent volume claim where for each disk, we define:
    • Access mode -> ReadWriteMany
    • Volume mode -> Block
    • Storage Class -> RAID1-FTT1
  • Then comes the roles of the vSphere CSI driver, which acknowledges that the Supervisor has the shared-disk capability, and creates a shared raw block volume on vSAN.
  • To realize the results, each Windows server will see an ordinary SCSI disk, and the cluster uses SCSI-3 persistent reservations to decide which node owns it, which is the job of the Failover Cluster mechanism.

How to build this?

Given that the underlying consumption layer will always remain the same, we can build this using 3 methods:

item.content:encoded:
Walk the halls of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 in Salt Lake City, and you’ll notice a subtle but unmistakable shift in how engineers talk about AI. A year ago, the dominant question was whether Kubernetes could handle AI workloads at all. This year, nobody is debating capability anymore. Instead they’re wrestling with the messy reality of running AI in production.

The conversations in Salt Lake City kept circling back to a single tension: enterprises want the speed of autonomous AI, but they aren’t willing to burn down their existing security, governance, and operational models to get it. Here is where the cloud-native ecosystem is actually heading.

AI Infrastructure Is Growing Up and Moving Into the Core

If there was any doubt that AI has become central to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation’s (CNCF) roadmap, the numbers settled it. In its 2026 ecosystem milestones announcement, CNCF reported that its portfolio has reached 231 hosted projects, with 32 added over the past year alone.

What stands out isn’t just the volume of new projects, though, but it’s what they’re trying to solve. With newcomers like Agent Substrate, OpenShell, and OpenRL, alongside llm-d 1.0 and HAMi’s move into incubation, the community is shifting from “how do we schedule a GPU?” to “how do we manage inference routing, accelerator sharing, and agent execution at scale?”

The real bottleneck for enterprises now isn’t a lack of tooling; it’s integration. Nobody wants to maintain a bespoke, disconnected infrastructure stack just to serve models. The winning pattern emerging from KubeCon is embedding GPU scheduling, isolation, and observability directly into the same Kubernetes control plane teams already trust.

Platform Engineering Has a New User…and It Isn’t Human

Platform engineering has officially gone mainstream. According to CNCF’s State of Cloud Native Development Q3 2026 report, 93% of developers now work inside organizations using some form of DevOps standardization or internal developer platform, up from 77% just a year ago.

Just as platform teams figured out how to build great self-service portals for human developers, however, a completely different kind of consumer showed up: autonomous AI agents.

Agents don’t click through dashboards or read internal wikis. They hit APIs directly, chain tools together, and trigger operational changes across systems in milliseconds. Trying to govern an autonomous agent with workflows designed for humans is a recipe for trouble. Projects like OpenShell and the broader push around agent identity point to where platform engineering has to go next while treating agents as first-class workloads by solving three core governance questions:

  1. Identity and Authorization: How are agent credentials managed and strictly scoped?
  2. Delegation: How is authority safely passed across distributed services without over-privileging the agent?
  3. Auditability: How are autonomous actions observed and logged in real time?

Conformance Needs to Move Up the Stack

As Kubernetes stretches to absorb AI, virtualization, and edge workloads, portability is once again front and center. Passing baseline Kubernetes conformance tells you a cluster meets the spec, but it doesn’t guarantee your workload won’t break when you move it between environments.

That’s why two complementary milestones at KubeCon matter so much. First, the Kubernetes AI Conformance Program hit 40 certified platforms, giving teams a reliable baseline for AI-ready infrastructure. VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) is among the platforms certified under the program, providing enterprises with a conformant Kubernetes runtime integrated into VMware Cloud Foundation. With support for GPU-enabled workloads, automated cluster lifecycle management, and enterprise security controls, VKS provides a foundation for running AI applications and emerging agentic workloads, including those built using technologies such as Agent Substrate. 

Second, the emerging Kubernetes Workload Conformance Working Group is tackling the harder half of the problem: ensuring that security, networking, storage, and resource behavior stay predictable for the application itself across different clusters.

Conformance is only part of the equation. Enterprises also need flexibility in choosing the tools that support their applications. Broadcom’s expanding VKS ISV partner ecosystem brings validated solutions across security, observability, networking, storage, and AI, helping organizations build production-ready Kubernetes environments without being limited to a single vendor’s tooling.

Preserving that kind of architectural choice is also what drives Broadcom’s upstream work. The VM API project, newly accepted into the CNCF Sandbox, is developing a provider-neutral Kubernetes API for virtual machine lifecycle management, enabling teams to manage VMs using the same declarative workflows they use for containers without tying the API to a single infrastructure provider. 

KubeVM Service brings this approach to VMware Cloud Foundation, allowing teams to provision and manage native vSphere VMs through Kubernetes and GitOps while retaining existing virtualization capabilities, operational visibility, and governance. For a closer look at how these technologies work together, see How VM API and KubeVM Service Deliver Open Standards and Enterprise Execution. You can also read more about how we’re approaching VM and workload portability in Advancing the Cloud-Native Ecosystem Through Open Collaboration.

Operational Resilience and Open-Source Sustainability

It’s easy to get distracted by shiny new agent frameworks at KubeCon, but stateful AI pipelines still live and die by unglamorous fundamentals like storage and disaster recovery. Upstream progress on Velero 1.19 which brings block-level incremental backup and restore and the Container Object Storage Interface (COSI) reflects a simple truth: you can’t claim production readiness for AI if you can’t reliably back up, move, and recover the data feeding it.

Just as important is the human capacity behind the code. The global cloud-native developer population reached 21.2 million in 2026. While AI-assisted coding is making it easier than ever to open a pull request, flooding open-source repositories with generated code puts massive strain on maintainers. Watching CNCF recognize mentors and documentation leaders at the 2026 Community Awards was a timely reminder that sustainable governance and human review (not just code velocity) are what keep this ecosystem resilient.

Looking Toward 2027

If KubeCon NA 2026 proved anything, it’s that the experimentation phase is over. Enterprises don’t need another standalone AI tool. What they do need are unified platforms, predictable workload portability, and battle-tested operational controls.

At Broadcom, our focus across upstream projects like VM API, Velero, COSI, and workload conformance comes down to helping teams bridge that gap without sacrificing openness. (For a full recap of our technical sessions and demos from the show floor, check out AI, Kubernetes, and Cloud Native Innovations: Broadcom at KubeCon North America 2026.) 

Heading into 2027, the real winners in cloud native won’t be the teams running the most experiments; they’ll be the ones who figured out how to make those experiments boring, repeatable, and safe in production.

item.content:encoded:
Server memory prices have surged over the past year, with some DRAM modules rising as much as 60% in a single month and no meaningful relief until 20271 and prices for server vendors are under even more pressure as lead times stretch from weeks to months2. Glencore, one of the world’s largest diversified natural resource companies, responded by deploying NVMe memory tiering, a standard capability in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), across its global infrastructure. The feature pairs DRAM with high-capacity NVMe solid-state drives in a single memory pool, and it has already doubled available memory in key Glencore environments without a matching rise in DRAM spend. It’s running in production today, and the business case gets stronger every time memory prices climb.

A global operation feeling the squeeze

Glencore produces and markets more than 60 commodities across 70 vCenters and roughly 50 locations worldwide. When a server procurement quote more than tripled in price in a matter of months, the infrastructure team got direct confirmation that DRAM-only provisioning was becoming financially untenable. A metro cluster resilience requirement at the Baar, Switzerland headquarters compounded the problem by capping usable DRAM at 50% of any host’s capacity (see the full case study for the metro cluster details).

How NVMe memory tiering works

VCF combines fast DRAM (Tier 0) with NVMe solid-state drives (Tier 1) into one memory pool, keeping hot data on DRAM and shifting cold data to NVMe automatically. A 1.6-terabyte NVMe drive costs roughly what 64 gigabytes of DRAM costs, so Glencore’s standard 1:1 DRAM-to-NVMe configuration doubles total memory for a fraction of the price. Broadcom’s own VCF 9.0 performance testing backs this up: a performance cost below 10% across enterprise benchmarks, up to double virtual machine density, and total cost of ownership savings of up to 40%. The full case study walks through Glencore’s own cost math in more depth.

From careful test to standard practice

Figure 1: Glencore mining operations

Glencore didn’t rush this. The team tested memory tiering on vSphere 8 first, then moved to the latest VCF release, where it became a single cluster configuration setting instead of a manual process. A multi-site evaluation spanning Brisbane, Sydney, and Baar preceded production, and the team retired its test environments once VCF 9.1 early access became available. The result: every new Cisco UCS server Glencore deploys now ships with an NVMe card built in. The case study covers the evaluation path step by step.

Results: more memory, lower costs, no developer complaints

Today, 50% of Glencore’s Linux developer VDI systems run on VCF NVMe memory tiering in production, with roughly 5% of all workloads in the Baar cluster using it so far, an early-stage number, not a ceiling. Standard VDI builds reserve 48 to 96 gigabytes of RAM per desktop even though utilization typically runs 10% to 15%, which is exactly the gap NVMe tiering closes without the matching DRAM outlay. Glencore is now extending the capability beyond VDI into business applications and databases. See the full case study for the complete workload breakdown.

Why this matters for infrastructure budgets right now

This isn’t a one-year pricing blip. TrendForce and Counterpoint Research both expect DRAM contract prices to climb 80-95% quarter-over-quarter into 2026 as AI data center demand keeps competing with enterprise IT for the same memory supply. Glencore’s approach, a disciplined evaluation, a staged rollout, and a hardware standard that compounds savings with every refresh, offers a template for any infrastructure team watching memory eat a growing share of its budget.

item.content:encoded:
The use of extra hardware has been a common element in migrations and upgrades. Extra servers would be provisioned as a new vSphere or vSAN cluster, and workloads would be moved over using vMotion and storage vMotion. It was the de facto approach for migrating from vSAN OSA to vSAN ESA, since no classic in-place migration between the two architectures exist.

But the pricing and availability of hardware in the data center has demanded a more prudent approach. Customers have shared with us that they clearly understand the benefit that vSAN ESA delivers, but are now looking for a leaner, minimalist path to transition their workloads and data to ESA. New capabilities within vSAN now make migrations from OSA to ESA easier and more cost efficient!

A Classic Swing Migration

Our telemetry data shows a large percentage of VMware customers running vSphere or vSAN OSA have servers that fully support vSAN ESA. Many of these servers running OSA already use NVMe storage devices in place—one of the primary requirements for ESA. Other servers often have the appropriate NVMe backplane, and just need NVMe storage devices to be ready for ESA.

The primary migration method used in the scenario described above was a classic swing migration. As shown in “Scenario 2 > Migration Option 2” in the post “Migrating to the Express Storage Architecture in vSAN,” three to six extra hosts were used to create a new cluster followed by a vMotion and storage vMotion migration of the workloads off of the old cluster to the new cluster. When sufficient resources were free on the old cluster, the remaining hosts would be decommissioned and reprovisioned as hosts in the new vSAN ESA cluster.

Figure 1. Classic swing migration from vSAN OSA to ESA

While this strategy is very simple, some found its inherent limitations difficult to overcome, including:

  • A lack of extra swing hosts to perform this migration. The cost and availability of hardware has meant that for many customers, there are no eligible extra hosts available for this task.
  • Insufficient swing hosts to maintain required levels of resilience. Some organizations have a strict requirement on higher levels of resilience, which means they must start with a cluster of six hosts instead of just three.
  • Insufficient rack space and network uplinks to accommodate swing hosts. Rack space and network uplinks can also be at a premium, especially when trying to place hosts in the appropriate leaf of a spine-leaf network.
  • Logistics of moving VM instances and data at the same time. This type of migration previously required the VM instance and the storage must be migrated at the same time. This could be a heavy lift depending on the circumstances.

A New Decoupled Swing Migration

vSAN in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1 introduced more flexibility with mounting remote datastores, where vSAN OSA clusters can mount the datastore of vSAN ESA clusters, and vice versa. One can use this capability to perform a decoupled swing migration, where workloads can be migrated from one cluster to another with minimal spare resources. Depending on the circumstances, this decoupled swing migration requires no extra hardware using swing hosts, and is very close in principle to an in-place upgrade of a cluster from OSA to ESA.

Not only will this migration method allow you to potentially avoid the use of swing hosts, but it will also maintain full data resilience of your workloads. Traditional swing migrations were more susceptible to temporary degradations in resilience as cluster host counts changed.

What the Workflow Looks Like

In this example, we will use a vSAN OSA cluster consisting of 20 hosts, with a high amount of CPU utilization, and ~40% storage capacity used. The hosts are fully compatible with ESA, but are running vSAN OSA. This particular example will not use any extra hardware as swing hosts, and have a maximum of only one host’s worth of compute resources offline (N-1) at any given time.

  1. Enter one host into maintenance mode, remove any disk claiming for that host, and remove it from the OSA cluster.
  2. Create a new vSAN ESA cluster, and move this “host 1” into a new vSAN ESA cluster. For the first eight hosts, do not claim any of the disks in yet, as it will only be providing compute resources initially.
  3. Mount the OSA cluster’s datastore to the new vSAN ESA cluster using the datastore sharing feature in 9.1.
  4. Perform a vMotion (compute only) of running VMs onto this first host. This allows the data to remain fully resilient on the new cluster as it is initially being provisioned.
  5. Repeat the process above, one host at a time, until 8 hosts have been moved to the new vSAN ESA cluster. At this point, the OSA cluster will be consuming about 67% of the available cluster capacity.
  6. Claim all of the appropriate storage devices for the hosts in the 8-host vSAN ESA cluster. Auto-RAID in vSAN for VCF 9.1 will automatically set the highest level of data resilience for you. Mount the ESA cluster’s datastore to the vSAN OSA cluster using the datastore sharing feature in 9.1.
  7. From the ESA cluster, perform a storage vMotion of all VM objects from the OSA cluster to the ESA cluster.
  8. For the ninth host in the OSA cluster, enter the host into maintenance mode, remove any disk claiming for that host, and remove it from the OSA cluster. Add this host to the new ESA cluster and claim the appropriate storage devices.
  9. Perform a vMotion (compute only) of one host’s worth of VM workloads.
  10. Repeat steps 8 and 9, until all of the remaining hosts in the OSA cluster have been migrated to the ESA cluster.
  11. Enable the Automatic Rebalance capability in the new vSAN ESA cluster.

Figure 2. Decoupled swing migration from vSAN OSA to ESA without using extra hardware (video)

In this particular scenario, there was never more than one host’s worth of compute capacity offline at any point. The initial 20-host OSA cluster required a substantial amount of free capacity because the cluster capacity decreased significantly during the initial 8-host cluster provisioning process, as shown in step 5, above. The initial capacity utilization, the overall cluster host count, and other variables will impact what is possible using this type of migration that does not use any extra swing hosts.

Who Can Benefit

A decoupled swing migration of workloads to a new vSAN ESA cluster using existing hardware is ideal for customers who:

  • Currently have vSAN OSA clusters using server hardware compatible with vSAN ESA.
  • Currently have vSAN OSA clusters with high workload CPU utilization, but relatively low storage capacity utilization.
  • Currently have little to no extra server hardware or rack space to help with migration from vSAN OSA to ESA.
  • Prefer to decouple the migration of VM instances (via vMotion) from VM storage (via storage vMotion).
  • Must maintain the prescribed levels of resilience during the migration.

Requirements and Caveats

While this more granular method of migration can minimize the need for spare hardware resources, it can introduce additional steps and other considerations, including, but not limited to:

  • Cluster host count. This decoupled swing migration is ideal for larger cluster sizes similar to the example shown above. Larger cluster host counts help keep the percentage of resources absent to a minimum while the migration process takes place.
  • Storage capacity utilization in cluster. A decoupled swing migration requires sufficient free storage capacity on the cluster. This is because several hosts that contribute storage capacity must first be removed from the cluster.
  • vSAN version. This decoupled swing migration uses a feature introduced in vSAN for VCF 9.1.
  • Hardware. The server hardware must be compatible with vSAN ESA. For some environments where the hardware is not already compatible, this may be as little as replacing the storage devices to NVMe storage devices during the decoupled swing migration.

Much like the traditional swing migration, the decoupled swing migration does not apply to first class disks (CNS persistent volumes for Kubernetes), vSAN file services shares, and vSAN iSCSI volumes. This data will need to be migrated independent from this migration prior to the OSA cluster being retired. The vSAN Performance Service on the OSA cluster must also be turned off before the OSA cluster can be fully decommissioned.

Recommendation: On the new ESA cluster, do not enable the “Automatic Rebalance” service until the migration has been completed. This will minimize any unnecessary rebalancing until after the migration procedure is complete.

Let’s Hear from You!

The vSAN Product Team is interested if streamlining this process would be useful for your environment. Please take this brief survey to help us better understand your specific environment, and how we can help you accomplish these types of OSA-to-ESA migrations easier.

Summary

There is a good chance that your server hardware running vSAN OSA can run vSAN ESA as well. Thanks to new capabilities in vSAN for VCF 9.1, a decoupled swing migration can make this transition easier and more cost-efficient than ever before. For more information on migrating to vSAN, see the vSAN Migration Guide.
